newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-UK's Brown gets warm EU welcome, rejects ERM.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK's Brown gets warm EU welcome, rejects ERM.

text.p: Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown received a warm reception from his European Union finance colleagues on Monday but wasted no time in laying out his agenda.

For starters, Brown said he had no plans to take the pound back into the European exchange rate mechanism. Sterling was dumped ignominiously from the ERM in September 1992, forced out by a flood of currency speculation.
"There has been no change in our position," Brown told reporters after his first roundtable session with EU finance ministers. "We have no plans to rejoin the ERM."
Brown's statement went a long way to dismiss reports last week that Britain was considering rejoining the ERM at a central rate of 2.50 marks.

Despite strong denials from the Treasury the pound, trading well above 2.80 marks before the report, went into a tailspin, dropping more than 10 pfennigs. It had recovered some poise on Monday and leapt two pfennigs after Brown's remarks.
Brown reportedly took some time to shake all the proffered hands at the start of Monday's meeting and responded by promising "a positive and constructive" approach to EU negotiations.
But cracks appeared even at the first meeting.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said there was no question of waiving the Maastricht Treaty rule that a currency must be part of the ERM for two years to make it eligible for a single European currency.
Brown, however, asked if the two-year rule was set in stone, replied simply: "No."
That argument is likely to be academic because Labour leaders have made no secret of the fact they think UK membership of EMU in the first wave, set for January 1999, is highly unlikely.
Brown again trotted out his mantra on European economic and monetary union on Monday, saying the decision would be made according to the strict economic tests he has set.
Britain's new Chancellor, in office for just over a week, succeeded in persuading the European Commission that a planned cut of VAT on domestic fuel bills met with EU laws.

"Although the Commission's legal analysis can only be completed once the full details are known, I do not see any particular legal obstacle at this stage," said Mario Monti, European Commissioner in charge of taxation.

EU sources had suggested Brown's plan to cut VAT on fuel to five percent from eight in his first budget, due within weeks, was against the spirit of EU law. But Brown had always said he would push ahead regardless.
EU leaders were keen to stress the positive aspects of Brown's first visit.

French finance minister Jean Arthuis noted Brown's measures to give the Bank of England independence to set interest rates and his commitment to meet the Maastricht targets on inflation and debt. "If he wanted to give positive signals, he is going the right way about it," he said.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said of Labour's election victory: "It is good news as far as the general atmosphere is concerned. It is more open-minded."
Brown's commitment to completing the single market also went down well, raising hopes of real progress at the inter-governmental conference summit in Amsterdam in June.
EU monetary affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said Brown had also "underlined his wish to work in a constructive manner on the euro."
Britain's Conservative government had blocked progress on various legal issues surrounding the euro, which required a unanimous vote.

But despite the efforts at compromise, Brown made it clear not everything was up for grabs in Amsterdam. Aside from Britain's wariness about EMU, he said there was no question of giving up the veto on taxation policies.
